activities.name: Using Python Lab: Notebook, Console, and scripts
activities.section_name: Chapter 0 — Starting Python and Python Lab
activities.content:
The supported Python environment

Moodle contains explanations, learning checks, and assignments; Python Lab executes the code. Opening “Python Lab 00” from Moodle leads to 00_start_here.ipynb in the learner workspace. Even on a shared computer, the file is stored in the server-side workspace opened through the browser, so learners do not install Python separately on each PC.

Python can be run in several ways. A Console accepts one instruction at a time. A .py script normally runs a saved sequence from top to bottom. A Notebook keeps explanation, code, and visible results together in cells. Because that record supports both practice and review, the Notebook is the course standard.

MethodBest suited toCourse use
Console (interactive mode)Trying a short expression or instruction immediatelySmall experiments when useful
.py scriptRunning a saved sequence of instructionsUnderstand common Python execution
NotebookKeeping explanation, code, and results togetherStandard for examples, practice, and submissions

Run the first cell

A Notebook has Markdown cells for prose and Code cells for Python. Select a Code cell and press Shift+Enter; Python runs that cell and returns the result below it. The following code displays text and then a calculated value.

print("Python Lab is ready")
print(3 + 4)

The quoted part on the first line is text to display. On the second line, 3 + 4 is calculated before it is displayed. Do not try to memorise the syntax yet. Change one value, rerun the cell, and observe what changes.

Running state and the saved Notebook

When a Code cell runs, the Python kernel keeps values in memory. The number beside a cell records actual execution order, not its position on the page. Running a later cell first can therefore create a state that another reader cannot reproduce from top to bottom.

If the visible results stop matching the explanation, restart the kernel and run every cell from the top. This checks that the Notebook is reproducible from a clean state. Saving with Ctrl+S preserves code, prose, and visible results in the Notebook file. Temporary kernel state and the saved file are not the same thing.

An error is evidence about the next step

An unclosed quote prevents Python from reading an instruction and produces SyntaxError. Valid syntax that uses an unknown name fails during execution with NameError. In both cases, the final traceback line gives an exception name and a concise message. Read that line first, inspect the named cell, change one thing, and run it again.

A program can also run and return the wrong answer. If a task says “three days, four sessions per day”, 3 + 4 runs and returns 7, but it does not represent the task. Successful execution and a correct result are different, which is why you predict before running and explain after checking.

Complete Python Lab 00

  1. Open 00_start_here.ipynb and run its Code cells from the top.
  2. Change one value, rerun it, and explain the changed result in a Markdown cell.
  3. Observe the prepared syntax and runtime errors and read the exception name on the final line.
  4. Restart the kernel and run all cells from the top.
  5. Save, close, and reopen the Notebook to confirm that your change remains.

Once this works, the next chapter can focus on Python rather than setup. If the workspace will not open or the server does not respond, do not change the managed environment. Report the Moodle activity name and the final visible error line to the teacher or administrator.

Estimated study time: 45–60 minutes

activities.name: Lesson 1.1: Programs, values, expressions, and output
activities.content:
Read the first program

Python Lab is ready, so begin with a short program. This example represents a course that runs three times a day for five days, with sixteen places in each session. Before running it, predict the three displayed lines.

print("Course delivery plan")
print(3 * 5)
print(3 * 5 * 16)

The Python interpreter normally executes these instructions from top to bottom. The first line displays a heading, the second displays 15 sessions, and the third displays 240 available places. Reading a program means tracing the instructions that produced a result, not merely looking at the result.

TermIn this exampleRole
Instructionprint(...)States an operation for the computer to perform
Value3, 5, 16, and the heading textData handled by the program
Expression3 * 5 * 16Evaluates to one value
OutputThe three displayed linesMakes a processed result visible outside the program

An expression makes a value; print() makes it visible

The expression 3 * 5 evaluates to the value 15. Passing that value to print() makes 15 appear on screen. Evaluation and output are two separate operations.

A Notebook helpfully displays 3 * 5 when it is the final expression in a cell. A normal .py script does not display that expression by itself. Use print() for an intended program output so that the intention remains clear in a Notebook, Console, or script.

The kind of value changes what an operator means

These two lines look similar but do not produce the same result.

print(3 + 4)
print("3 + 4")

On the first line, 3 and 4 are numeric values, so + adds them and produces 7. On the second, everything inside the quotes is a text value, so the characters 3 + 4 are displayed unchanged. Every value has a kind that determines sensible operations. Later lessons develop type names and conversion systematically; for now, distinguish numbers from quoted text.

Express the intended order of calculation

This lesson uses only addition +, subtraction -, and multiplication *. Multiplication is evaluated before addition or subtraction, while parentheses are evaluated first.

print(2 + 3 * 4)
print((2 + 3) * 4)

The first expression is 14 because 3 * 4 is evaluated first. The second is 20 because the parentheses produce 5 before multiplication. Even when you know precedence, parentheses can make work meaning explicit. To subtract morning 18 and afternoon 12 from capacity 40, 40 - (18 + 12) clearly says to combine attendance before finding unused places.

Changing a value exposes a weakness

The following program displays morning and afternoon places, their total, and unused capacity.

print("Workshop places")
print("Morning:", 18)
print("Afternoon:", 12)
print("Total:", 18 + 12)
print("Unused seats:", 40 - (18 + 12))

Predict all five lines, then run the cell from the top. Now change the morning places to 20. Because the value 18 is written directly in three locations, all three must be edited or the outputs contradict each other. Python cannot infer that those three values have the same meaning. Lesson 2 gives the value one name and makes this kind of change safer.

If the code will not run, check for a missing closing quote or parenthesis. If it runs, check that total and unused seats can both be true. The Chapter 0 distinction between syntax, execution, and a result that meets the purpose applies here.

Create your own program

Suppose each box contains twelve learning books and four full boxes are prepared. Display a heading, books per box, number of boxes, and total books on four clearly labelled lines. Use only numbers, text, *, parentheses, and print(). Change the box count to five and explain in a Markdown cell which lines needed editing.

After this lesson, you can point to an instruction, value, expression, and output in a short program and predict its execution from the top. The learning check uses running code rather than definition recall alone. Lesson 2 then gives values names and introduces changing program state.

Estimated study time: about 2 hours

[v1 attempt archive - hidden] Knowledge check: Lesson 1: Your first Python program
Knowledge check: 1.1 Programs, values, expressions, and output
Lesson 1.2: Variables, assignment, and program state
activities.content:
Keep one source for one meaning

At the end of Lesson 1, the morning count 18 was written directly in several expressions. Changing it to 20 required several edits, and a missed edit could make the outputs contradict each other. Give the value one name instead.

capacity = 40
morning = 18
afternoon = 12

print("Total:", morning + afternoon)
print("Unused seats:", capacity - (morning + afternoon))

When morning = 18 runs, Python first evaluates 18 on the right and makes the name morning refer to that value. This operation is assignment. Later expressions read morning instead of repeating 18. Changing the morning count now requires one edit, and both outputs use the same information.

Assignment is not mathematical equality

One = in Python does not assert that both sides are equal. It evaluates the right-hand side, then assigns the result to the name on the left. Two signs, ==, ask whether values are equal.

registered = 40
print(registered == 40)
print(registered == 35)

The first line creates state; the other lines compare without changing it. They display True and False. Booleans and decisions are developed later, but distinguishing = from == matters now.

Read the right side before updating the left

A name can later be assigned another value. This is reassignment. Trace the value of total after every line.

total = 12
amount = 5
total = total + amount
print(total)

On the third line, total on the right is still 12. Python adds 12 and 5 to make 17, then updates the name on the left. Read the line as “add the amount to the current total, then make that result the new total”, not as an algebraic equation.

The same update can be written total += amount. The shorter spelling still reads the current values before updating the left name. This course uses the long form until the state change is clear.

A calculated value does not update itself

Assignment connects a name to the result produced when that line runs. It is not a spreadsheet formula that recalculates automatically whenever an input changes.

planned = 15
cancelled = 2
delivered = planned - cancelled

cancelled = 4
print("Cancelled:", cancelled)
print("Delivered:", delivered)

delivered became 13 on the third line. Changing cancelled to 4 does not change the already calculated value, so delivered remains 13. Run delivered = planned - cancelled again to update it to 11. Understanding which calculations must run after a state change is a foundation for reliable programs.

A name follows rules and communicates meaning

Names explain code to its readers. completed_learners communicates more than x, but an identifier cannot be arbitrary prose.

NameValid?Reason
completed_learnersYesLetters and an underscore communicate meaning
group2YesA digit is allowed after the first character
2nd_groupNoAn identifier cannot start with a digit
completed learnersNoAn identifier cannot contain a space
classNoIt is a Python keyword

Names are case-sensitive, so Score and score are different. Ordinary variables normally use lower-case words and underscores. All capitals, as in MAX_SEATS, signal a convention that the value should not change; Python does not enforce that convention.

Use NameError to inspect execution order

Reading a name that has not yet been assigned, is misspelled, or differs in case normally raises NameError. Read the exception name and message on the final traceback line, then compare the names character by character.

completed_learners = 29
print(completed_learner)

The second name is missing its final s. In a Notebook, the same error can occur when the correct assignment cell is visible but has not run. Check both spelling and whether the required assignment executed first.

Make Notebook state reproducible

The kernel remembers names created by earlier cell execution. A Notebook may therefore work on your screen after cells were run out of order but fail for a reader who starts at the top. Before saving, restart the kernel and run every cell from the top. This proves that each required assignment appears before use and that the Notebook has no hidden state dependency.

From guided example to transfer

A learning centre planned 15 sessions and cancelled 2. Use planned, cancelled, and delivered to display all three. Predict state after every line, change cancelled to 4, and explain in Markdown which calculation must run again to update delivery correctly.

Then give meaningful names to room capacity 24, morning use 18, and afternoon use 20. Display unused places for both periods. Change the single capacity assignment to 22, restart the kernel, run all cells, and confirm that unused places become 4 and 2.

After this lesson, you can trace assignment from the right, explain state after reassignment, distinguish = from ==, and diagnose NameError and Notebook execution order. The next lesson systematically develops the basic data types referred to by these names.

Estimated study time: about 2 hours

activities.name: Python Lab 1.2: Variables, assignment, and state
Knowledge check: 1.2 Variables, assignment, and program state
Lesson 1.5: Decisions with conditions
activities.content:
After calculating a value, choose what the program should do with it

You can now create values, store them in variables, convert text and numbers, and display a meaningful result. Operational work also requires choices. A centre with a low completion rate may need support, while a centre on track receives an ordinary report. Python represents this choice with an if statement.

A condition produces the Boolean value True or False

A comparison such as score >= 50 produces a value of type bool: either True or False. = assigns the value on its right to a name; == compares two values for equality. This small distinction prevents a common class of decision errors.

score = 68
print(score >= 50)
print(score == 68)
print(score != 68)
print(type(score >= 50))
OperatorDecision
== / !=equal / not equal
< / <=less than / at most
> / >=greater than / at least

if runs its indented block only when the condition is True

A colon ends if condition:. Indentation on the next line places that statement inside the if block. In Python, indentation is not decoration; it defines program structure.

score = 68
if score >= 50:
    print("Pass")
print("Decision complete")

For 68, both lines appear. For 42, Pass is skipped but the unindented Decision complete still runs. Read every statement in relation to its indentation.

else selects exactly one of two actions

else handles the case in which the preceding condition is False. The if and else blocks cannot both run during one decision.

score = 42
if score >= 50:
    result = "Pass"
else:
    result = "Review"
print(result)

elif checks several candidates from the top and selects the first match

Use elif for three or more possible results. Python tests conditions from the top and stops after the first True branch. When conditions overlap, put the more selective rule first.

score = 85
if score >= 90:
    grade = "Excellent"
elif score >= 70:
    grade = "Pass"
elif score >= 50:
    grade = "Conditional pass"
else:
    grade = "Review"
print(grade)

If score >= 50 came first, 85 would match it and never reach a higher category. Code can run without an exception while still implementing the wrong operational rule.

Independent if statements run independently

Two separate if statements can both run. An if / elif / else chain chooses one candidate. Separate statements fit “send a pass notice and also award merit”; one chain fits “assign one grade category.”

score = 80
if score >= 50:
    print("Send pass notice")
if score >= 70:
    print("Award merit")

and, or, and not combine decisions

and is True when both operands are True; or when at least one is True; not reverses a Boolean value. Split a long condition into meaningful names so that each intermediate result can be inspected.

registered = 35
completion_rate = 72
has_enough_learners = registered >= 30
rate_needs_support = completion_rate < 75
priority = has_enough_learners and rate_needs_support
print(has_enough_learners, rate_needs_support, priority)

Comparisons bind before not, then and, then or. Rather than forcing a reader to recall precedence, use parentheses and named parts to make the intended grouping visible.

Test immediately below, at, and above each boundary

>= 50 includes 50; > 50 does not. For thresholds at 75 and 85, try 74.9, 75, 84.9, and 85. Python also permits the range comparison 0 <= score <= 100.

rate = 75
if rate < 75:
    status = "priority support"
elif rate < 85:
    status = "monitor"
else:
    status = "on track"
print(status)

Validate the value before applying ordinary categories

Classifying a score of -5 as merely “Review” produces code that runs but a result that is wrong. Check the permitted domain first, then apply the ordinary classification.

score = -5
if not 0 <= score <= 100:
    result = "Invalid score"
elif score >= 50:
    result = "Pass"
else:
    result = "Review"
print(result)

Short-circuit evaluation skips an expression after the result is known

and skips its right operand when the left is False; or skips its right operand when the left is True. The following guard avoids division by zero because registration is zero. Use this for clear safety checks, but do not hide updates or other side effects inside a condition.

registered = 0
completed = 0
if registered > 0 and completed / registered >= 0.75:
    status = "on track"
else:
    status = "needs review"
print(status)

From guided example to transfer

Classify a learning centre from registered learners, completed learners, and whether an absence report exists. A negative count or completions above registrations means data review. An absence report or completion below 75% means priority support. Below 85% means monitor; otherwise it is on track. Test invalid data and cases corresponding to 74.9%, 75%, 84.9%, and 85%, reaching every branch.

After this lesson, you can explain comparisons and bool, indentation, ordered branches, independent if statements, and/or/not, boundaries, validation, and short-circuit evaluation. The next lesson applies the same processing repeatedly with loops.

Estimated study time: about 3 hours

Lesson 1.6: Repetition with loops
activities.content:
Repeat one pattern accurately for every value

Conditions let a program select work for one value. Operational data contains several weeks, learners, or centres requiring the same pattern. Copying the code by hand makes additions and corrections fragile. A loop states the repeated operation once and supplies each target value in turn.

for takes one value at a time from an iterable

In for attendance in weekly_attendance:, each list item is assigned to attendance and the indented block runs. The loop variable is a temporary name for the current value. An unindented statement runs once after all iterations.

weekly_attendance = [28, 31, 32, 34]
for attendance in weekly_attendance:
    print("Attendance this week:", attendance)
print("Processing complete")

range() includes its start and excludes its stop

range(start, stop, step) produces integers. range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3, 4; five is excluded. range(4) gives zero through three. State the expected first value, last value, and iteration count before running to expose an off-by-one error.

print(list(range(1, 5)))
for week in range(1, 5):
    print(f"Week {week}")
print(list(range(10, 4, -2)))

Initialise an accumulator before the loop and update it inside

An accumulator preserves state across iterations. A total usually starts at zero and receives the current value each time. Initialising it inside the loop resets it on every iteration and leaves only the final item.

weekly_attendance = [28, 31, 32, 34]
total = 0
for attendance in weekly_attendance:
    total += attendance
    print("Running total:", total)
print("Total:", total)
print("Mean:", total / len(weekly_attendance))

sum() can calculate a simple total. Tracing an explicit loop first reveals how conditional aggregation and several simultaneous results work. In production code, prefer the readable built-in when a plain total is the whole task.

A counter increases by one only for a matching item

A counter also starts at zero. A total adds a value; a counter adds one item. Separate names keep these two roles clear.

weeks_at_least_30 = 0
for attendance in [28, 31, 32, 34]:
    if attendance >= 30:
        weeks_at_least_30 += 1
print(weeks_at_least_30)

Initialise a maximum from real data

Starting a maximum at zero fails when every observation is negative, returning a value that was not present. For known non-empty data, start with the first item. If empty data is possible, handle it explicitly before selecting the first item.

weekly_change = [-4, -2, -7, -3]
if weekly_change:
    largest = weekly_change[0]
    for change in weekly_change[1:]:
        if change > largest:
            largest = change
    print("Largest:", largest)
else:
    print("No data")

enumerate() supplies a number and value together

When output requires both a human-readable week number and its value, enumerate() is clearer than maintaining a manual counter. start=1 begins at Week 1.

weekly_attendance = [28, 31, 32, 34]
for week, attendance in enumerate(weekly_attendance, start=1):
    print(f"Week {week}: {attendance} learners")

continue skips this iteration; break ends the loop

continue skips the remaining work for the current value and advances. break ends the loop without processing later values. Use them for explicit reasons such as skipping a missing reading or stopping at a critical invalid value, rather than scattering jumps through ordinary work.

readings = [28, None, 31, -1, 34]
for reading in readings:
    if reading is None:
        continue
    if reading < 0:
        print("Invalid value found; stopping")
        break
    print("Valid value:", reading)

while repeats while its condition remains True

Use while when a stopping condition rather than a known collection controls repetition. The state used by the condition must change toward termination inside the loop, or the loop may never end. If a Notebook cell does not finish, interrupt it and inspect the condition and update.

remaining = 3
while remaining > 0:
    print("Remaining:", remaining)
    remaining -= 1
print("Complete")

Use for for known values and while for a changing stopping condition

Use for to process an iterable such as a list. Use while for work such as retrying until success or processing until a remaining count reaches zero. Indexing a known list with while requires manual initialisation, boundary checks, and updates, creating more places for errors.

An empty iterable runs a for loop zero times

A for loop over an empty list ends normally without entering its body. The total remains zero, but total / len(values) would divide by zero. Check the count after the loop and explicitly report that a mean does not exist.

values = []
total = 0
for value in values:
    total += value
if values:
    print(total / len(values))
else:
    print("No data")

From guided example to transfer

Process four weekly material costs [82.5, 74.0, 91.5, 80.0] in one for loop. Calculate total, mean, maximum, and the count of weeks above 80. Display each week with enumerate(). Then run an empty list without dividing and display No data. “Above 80” excludes exactly 80, so the condition and explanation must agree.

After this lesson, you can explain for, the excluded range endpoint, accumulators, counters, maximum initialisation, enumerate, continue/break, while termination, and empty data. The applied project combines these foundations in a weekly support report.

Estimated study time: about 3 hours

activities.content:
1.7 Mini-project: Weekly support report

What you will do

  1. Complete the TODOs in weekly_support.py in Python Lab.
  2. Enter the sample daily records below and inspect the result yourself.
  3. Run check_weekly_support.py and pass its eight checks.
  4. Submit only the completed weekly_support.py.

Situation

At the end of each day, a learning-centre staff member records received support requests and requests resolved that day. At week end, the staff member reads the Monday-to-Friday daily records and types the figures into the program. The program aggregates them and displays a weekly report.

Input and sample daily records

This table is not a CSV file and is not copied into the program. It is fictional data for checking the completed program. Run weekly_support.py, then type the values from top to bottom. The finished program must accept different figures each week.

DayReceivedResolved
Monday1210
Tuesday1816
Wednesday1515
Thursday2017
Friday109

For example, enter 12 at Monday received:, then 10 at Monday resolved:, and continue through Friday. This project uses manual input because file input has not yet been studied; later projects will read files.

Program requirements

The staff member enters the figures from the daily records. The program automates the totals, resolution-rate calculation, status decision, and identification of the busiest day. Display totals received and resolved, unresolved count, resolution rate to one decimal place, status, and busiest day. At least 90% is ON TRACK; at least 80% is REVIEW; below 80% is PRIORITY SUPPORT. On a busiest-day tie, keep the first day.

Implementation contract: This project practises repetition, so process the Monday-to-Friday inputs with one for loop. Do not write the same input code five times.

Expected output

WEEKLY SUPPORT REPORT
TOTAL RECEIVED: 75
TOTAL RESOLVED: 67
UNRESOLVED: 8
RESOLUTION RATE: 89.3%
STATUS: REVIEW
BUSIEST DAY: Thursday

Zero requests and invalid data

  • For zero total requests use rate N/A, status NO REQUESTS, and busiest day NONE.
  • A negative count or resolved above received is invalid.
  • Continue through Friday after an invalid value, then display only RESULT: INVALID; do not display the report heading or result fields.
  • Assume integer input in this project. Non-integer exception handling is studied later.

Python in scope

Use variables, integers, strings, input(), int(), print(), f-strings, arithmetic, comparisons, Boolean operators, if / elif / else, for, and range(). Functions, lists, dictionaries, classes, file input, and pandas are not required.

Hints
  1. How will you update two weekly totals after each input?
  2. How will you remember an invalid value until input finishes?
  3. Which comparison retains the first day on a tie?
  4. Which case must be handled before division?
  5. In what order should 80% and 90% be tested?

The starter has TODOs. Complete them and remove PROGRAM INCOMPLETE.

Checking

1. Check it yourself

Run the script, enter the ten sample values, and compare with the expected output.

From the Python Lab terminal:

python projects/weekly-support/weekly_support.py

2. Run the supplied checker

python projects/weekly-support/check_weekly_support.py

Do not change the checker. It checks a standard week, exactly 80%, exactly 90%, below 80%, a busiest-day tie, zero requests, resolved above received, and a negative count. Change only weekly_support.py when a result is NG.

Save, check, and submit

Save first

After editing weekly_support.py, always press Ctrl + S. Do not rely on automatic saving in this environment. Reloading the page before saving may discard your changes. Running, checking, and submitting use the last saved file.

  1. Complete the TODOs in weekly_support.py, then press Ctrl + S.
  2. Run the program, enter the ten sample values, and compare the result with the expected output.
  3. Run the checker.
    python projects/weekly-support/check_weekly_support.py
  4. When all eight items are OK and the last line is ALL TESTS PASSED, choose either submission method below.

Method A: Submit directly from Python Lab

Run the submission cell in the Project Notebook or the following command. The checker runs again. Only a passing, last-saved weekly_support.py is sent to the Moodle Assignment.

python /home/jovyan/work/projects/weekly-support/submit_weekly_support.py

SUBMISSION COMPLETE and a Moodle submission ID confirm success. Run the command again to resubmit the currently saved file.

Method B: Use Moodle's standard submission page

In Python Lab, right-click weekly_support.py in the file browser and download it. Then upload that file on the Moodle Assignment submission page and confirm the submission.

Deliverable and completion conditions

Submit only the completed weekly_support.py. Do not submit the Notebook, check_weekly_support.py, screenshots, or an essay.

  • The sample daily records produce the expected weekly report.
  • All eight checks are OK and the checker ends with ALL TESTS PASSED.
  • The saved weekly_support.py has been submitted to the Moodle Assignment by Method A or Method B.

Lesson 2.1: Lists, dictionaries, and records
activities.content:
Organise related values as one structure

Chapter 1 supplied weekly attendance in a list so a loop could process it. This lesson studies that list systematically, then combines fields with different meanings—name, registration, completion—into one record and several records.

A list is ordered and mutable

Create a list with brackets. Indexes begin at zero, negative indexes count from the end, and a slice excludes its end. len() returns the item count and in tests membership. Python permits mixed types, but operational lists are safer when their items share one meaning.

attendance = [28, 31, 30, 33]
print(attendance[0])
print(attendance[-1])
print(attendance[1:3])
print(len(attendance))
print(31 in attendance)

Modify a list through positions and mutation methods

Index assignment replaces an item. append() adds one item, extend() adds several, and insert() adds at a position. remove() deletes the first matching value; pop() removes and returns the value at a position.

attendance = [28, 31, 30]
attendance[0] = 29
attendance.append(33)
attendance.extend([32, 34])
removed = attendance.pop()
print(attendance)
print("Removed:", removed)

Most mutation methods, including append(), change the existing list and return None. Writing attendance = attendance.append(33) therefore replaces the useful name with None.

Assignment shares one list rather than duplicating it

After shared = original, both names refer to the same list. A mutation through either name is visible through both. Use copy() or a full slice for an independent shallow copy.

original = [28, 31, 30]
shared = original
separate = original.copy()
shared.append(33)
print("original:", original)
print("shared:", shared)
print("separate:", separate)

A shallow copy duplicates only the outer list. If it contains an inner list or dictionary, that inner object remains shared. When modifying nested data, identify which levels must be independent.

A tuple is ordered but immutable

Create a tuple with parentheses and read it by index or iteration. A fixed group such as report year and month should not have individual elements replaced. A tuple can also unpack into the same number of names.

report_period = (2026, 8)
year, month = report_period
print(year, month)
# report_period[0] = 2027  # TypeError

A dictionary names each field with a key

A dictionary stores key: value pairs in braces. Read by a meaningful key such as centre[\"registered\"], not a numeric position. Keys are unique: assignment to an existing key updates it, while assignment to a new key adds a field.

centre = {
    "name": "North Learning Centre",
    "district": "North",
    "registered": 40,
    "completed": 32,
}
centre["registered"] = 42
centre["phone"] = "000-000"
print(centre)

Handle a missing key according to the field meaning

Brackets raise KeyError for a missing key. For an optional phone field, get(\"phone\", \"not recorded\") can return a default. Do not silently replace a missing required registration with zero; missing and genuine zero mean different things. Use in and treat a missing required field as invalid data.

centre = {"name": "North", "registered": 40}
print(centre.get("phone", "not recorded"))
print("completed" in centre)

Select the dictionary view needed by the loop

A direct for loop over a dictionary yields keys. keys() also provides keys, values() provides values, and items() provides key-value pairs.

centre = {"registered": 40, "attended": 34, "completed": 32}
for field, value in centre.items():
    print(field, value)

A list of dictionaries represents several records

Treat one dictionary as one record and each key as a field name. A list of dictionaries with consistent keys behaves like a small table and forms a conceptual bridge to CSV files and DataFrames.

centres = [
    {"name": "North", "district": "A", "registered": 40, "completed": 32},
    {"name": "South", "district": "B", "registered": 35, "completed": 24},
]
for centre in centres:
    rate = centre["completed"] / centre["registered"] * 100
    print(f"{centre['name']}: {rate:.1f}%")

A set represents unique membership and supports set operations

A set focuses on presence rather than order or duplicates. Union |, intersection &, and difference - compare categories such as offered and requested courses. Never depend on set display order. Create an empty set with set().

offered = {"Python", "Data", "Office"}
requested = {"Python", "Web", "Data"}
print("Common:", offered & requested)
print("Not offered:", requested - offered)
print("All:", offered | requested)
StructureOrderedMutableMain use
listyesyessequence of similarly meaningful values
tupleyesnofixed group
dictinsertion orderyesnamed fields
setdo not depend on orderyesunique membership

Find one record by ID and distinguish absence

Match a unique ID rather than a position. Begin with None, store the matching dictionary, and break. If no match exists, None is the normal “not found” result.

found = None
for book in books:
    if book["id"] == target_id:
        found = book
        break

Add, read, update, and delete in one collection

Check an ID set before adding. A found dictionary is the dictionary stored in the list, so field assignment updates the record. Use enumerate() to find a removal position and pop() once, preserving remaining order. These operations form CRUD.

Transfer exercise: equipment register

Begin with three records containing asset_id, name, and available; add A004, update A002, remove A003, and search for an absent ID.

Additional practice: transfer to centre records

Store three centres as dictionaries containing name, district, registered, and completed, inside one list. Display every completion rate, append names below 75% to a separate list, and create a set of districts. Confirm that zero registration or a missing required key does not produce an ordinary rate.

After this lesson, you can choose structures using order, names, duplicates, and mutability, then combine lists and dictionaries to process records. The next lesson separates that processing into functions and introduces errors and tests.

Lesson 2.2: Functions, errors, and testing
activities.content:
Separate a long process into functions with clear responsibilities

Lesson 2.1 represented learning centres as a list of dictionaries. Now turn that one-off processing into named components that can be called repeatedly. A function does more than shorten code: it creates an explicit boundary around inputs, processing, and outputs so that one rule can be maintained and tested in one place.

Define with def, then call by name

Write the function name and parameters after def, followed by a colon. The indented body does not run when it is defined; it runs when called. The definition must execute before its call.

def completion_rate(completed, registered):
    return completed / registered * 100

rate = completion_rate(32, 40)
print(f"Completion rate: {rate:.1f}%")

Parameters are inputs and return is the output

Names in the definition are parameters; values supplied by a call are arguments. return sends a value to the caller and ends the function. print() only displays output. A function without an explicit return produces None, so return values needed by later calculations.

def add_with_print(a, b):
    print(a + b)

def add_with_return(a, b):
    return a + b

x = add_with_print(2, 3)
y = add_with_return(2, 3)
print(x, y * 2)

Local names keep processing contained

A variable assigned inside a function is normally local and cannot be read directly outside it. Receive required values through parameters and return results. This reduces accidental dependence on external state and makes the same behaviour easier to reproduce and test.

Defaults and keyword arguments make calls readable

Optional parameters can have defaults; put required parameters first. A keyword argument such as completed=32 makes meaning visible and reduces mistakes when several arguments have the same numeric type.

def format_centre(name, completed, registered, decimals=1):
    rate = completed / registered * 100
    return f"{name}: {rate:.{decimals}f}%"

print(format_centre("North", completed=32, registered=40))

Docstrings and type hints communicate a contract

A docstring states purpose, inputs, return value, and invalid-input policy. Type hints help readers and tools, but Python does not automatically enforce them at runtime. Validate conditions imposed by real operational data in code.

def safe_rate(completed: int, registered: int) -> float | None:
    """Return the completion rate, or None when registration is not positive."""
    if registered <= 0:
        return None
    return completed / registered * 100

Separate validation, calculation, and presentation

Mixing every responsibility into one long function obscures failures. Use separate functions to check required keys and ranges, calculate a rate, and prepare display. Raise KeyError for a missing required key and ValueError for a violated value rule so the caller receives a meaningful cause.

REQUIRED = {"name", "registered", "completed"}

def validate_centre(centre):
    missing = REQUIRED - centre.keys()
    if missing:
        raise KeyError(f"Missing required fields: {sorted(missing)}")
    if centre["completed"] > centre["registered"]:
        raise ValueError("Completed exceeds registered")

Classify errors by stage and read a traceback from the end

A syntax error prevents parsing, a runtime error raises an exception during execution, and a logic error runs but produces a wrong result. Start with the final traceback line for the exception name and message, then move upward to the relevant line in your code.

Keep try narrow and catch only expected exceptions

Catch a specific exception that the program can handle. else runs when no exception occurred and finally supports cleanup needed in either case. Do not use except Exception: pass, which hides the cause. Unexpected errors should remain visible so they can be fixed.

try:
    registered = int(raw_value)
except ValueError:
    print("Not a valid integer")
else:
    print(registered)
finally:
    print("Input check finished")

Test normal, boundary, and invalid cases separately

One normal case cannot expose boundary bugs. Include ordinary values, boundaries such as zero and threshold neighbours, and invalid cases such as missing keys and impossible ranges. State expectations with assert and compare floats with a small tolerance. Assertions are useful checks here but do not replace validation of user data.

assert abs(safe_rate(32, 40) - 80.0) < 0.0001
assert safe_rate(0, 0) is None
assert safe_rate(1, -1) is None

Define search and mutation contracts

Search absence returns None. A mutation changes and returns the stored dictionary, raising KeyError when the target is absent. Blank or duplicate additions violate a new-value rule and raise ValueError.

def mark_as_read(books, book_id):
    book = find_book(books, book_id)
    if book is None:
        raise KeyError(book_id)
    book["read"] = True
    return book

Test state before and after

Check count, order, and stored-object identity as well as the return. The supplied checker is another program that consumes this public contract. You need not author it yet, but must preserve filename, function names, returns, mutations, and exceptions.

Transfer exercise: equipment-register functions

Separate the 2.1 operations into search, add, update, and remove functions, then assert normal, absent, blank, duplicate, and before-and-after cases.

Additional practice: separate centre processing into functions

Use the three centres from 2.1 and separate the process into validate_centre(), centre_rate(), and summarise_centres(). The last function returns a dictionary containing names below 75%, the set of districts, total registration, and total completion. Test three valid records, zero registration, a missing required key, and completion above registration.

After this lesson, you can define a function contract, classify and communicate failures, and test representative boundaries. Lesson 2.3 combines these components into a monthly performance report.

Project 2.4 — CSV library record manager

1. Situation

A small learning centre stores its book catalogue in data/books.csv. A staff member has received four requests to update the catalogue. Build a program that loads the source CSV, applies those requests, counts the updated records, displays a report, and saves the result as a separate CSV.

2. What you will do

You do not create the program from an empty file. In Python Lab, open the supplied starter at projects/library-manager/library_manager.py and complete its ten unfinished functions. This Python program will read and process the CSV. Edit only library_manager.py.

  1. Make the Python program load the supplied books.csv (the sample contains four books).
  2. Apply four specified updates in order.
  3. Count the books after the updates.
  4. Save the updated records to books_updated.csv.
  5. Display the summary on screen.

Functions such as load_books() process any valid number of records rather than fixing the input at four books. However, this project's run_project() is specific to the supplied books.csv and applies the four update requests shown below.

3. Input CSV and source protection

The supplied projects/library-manager/data/books.csv contains:

id,title,read
B001,Python Basics,false
B002,Data Skills for Beginners,true
B003,Networks in Practice,false
B004,"Writing, Presenting, and Learning",true

This listing is provided so you can understand the input before opening the file. Do not copy it into the Python source. Read the supplied file with csv.DictReader.

The first row is the header. DictReader initially produces string values with the keys id, title, and read; parse_read() converts the read text to a bool. B004 shows that a field containing commas is quoted. Do not split lines yourself or remove the quotes yourself—the csv module handles them.

data/books.csv is the unchanged source record. Do not edit or overwrite it. Always save the result to output/books_updated.csv.

4. How to apply the four update requests

In a larger system, update requests might come from another file or a user interface. This project focuses on writing and combining update functions, so the four requests are not another file and are not keyboard input. Implement these fixed function calls directly inside run_project(), in this order:

add_book(books, "B005", "Algorithms Made Clear")
mark_as_read(books, "B003")
rename_book(books, "B001", "Python Foundations")
remove_book(books, "B004")

5. Before and after

Because B004 is later removed, the checker tests load_books() independently to confirm that its comma-containing title was read correctly.

6. Public contract for all ten functions

The starter also contains a completed main() in addition to the ten functions below. main() calls run_project() with the default paths and displays the returned summary. Do not rename or change main(). IDs and titles are stripped of surrounding whitespace before validation, search, or storage.

Ignore extra CSV columns. A completely empty file raises ValueError for missing columns; a correct header with no data rows returns an empty list. Do not sort during saving; preserve the current list order.

7. Path basis

The starter already constructs the input and output paths from the script's own folder. The program therefore finds its files regardless of the terminal's current directory. Do not change the constant names or default paths.

8. Implementation stages

  1. Complete parse_read() and load_books(); confirm four records and bool values.
  2. Complete find_book(); check a present and an absent ID.
  3. Complete add, rename, mark-read, and remove.
  4. Complete summarise_books().
  5. Complete save_books() and reload its output.
  6. In run_project(), connect load, updates, summary, save, and return in that order.
  7. Finish every TODO and delete the final print("PROGRAM INCOMPLETE") line.

activities.name: Lesson 3.1: Tabular data, CSV, and pandas
activities.content:
Treat a collection of records as an inspectable table

3.1.1 Tabular data — rows, columns, and cells

Lesson 2.3 processed one centre as a dictionary and several as a list. As records and fields grow, tabular data aligns the same columns across every record and supports column-level inspection and calculation. pandas represents this table as a DataFrame.

Align one observation per row and one variable per column

Here one row is one centre-month observation, one column is a variable with consistent meaning, and one cell is one variable value for one observation. Treat expected types, units, and missing-value rules together with column names as the schema. Mixing counts and text in one column makes later calculations unreliable.

3.1.2 CSV — a text format for exchanging tables

A CSV commonly has a header on its first line, records on later lines, and commas between fields. Values containing commas or newlines need quoting. CSV does not retain cell colours, formulas, or multiple sheets. Decide how to read encoding, delimiter, empty fields, and identifiers with meaningful leading zeros.

month,centre_id,centre_name,registered,completed
2026-01,C001,Gaborone Learning Centre,32,24
2026-01,C002,"North, Main Centre",27,18

Relative paths and the file actually loaded

data/learning-centres-practice.csv starts from the kernel working directory, not necessarily from the Notebook file. Different Python Lab entry points can therefore change what the same relative path means. The course helper checks the current location and parents, the server work area, and distributed materials, then prints the absolute path actually loaded. For FileNotFoundError, first read the working directory and checked paths.

from pathlib import Path
print("Working directory:", Path.cwd())
data_file = find_course_data("learning-centres-practice.csv")
print("Loading:", data_file.resolve())

Express read_csv assumptions in code

import pandas as pd is the conventional import. pd.read_csv() creates a DataFrame. Here UTF-8 is explicit, while centre_id and month remain strings rather than quantities. Another file may require a different sep or encoding.

df = pd.read_csv(
    data_file,
    encoding="utf-8",
    dtype={"centre_id": "string", "month": "string"},
)

3.1.3 pandas — load and inspect a DataFrame

Use head() for value layout, shape for row and column counts, columns for exact names, dtypes and info() for inferred types, and isna().sum() for missing counts. The practice CSV has 24 rows and 10 columns with deliberate quality issues. Loading successfully is not the same as loading correctly.

print(df.head(3))
print("Shape:", df.shape)
print(df.columns.tolist())
print(df.dtypes)
print(df.isna().sum())
df.info()

Display every row and count raw category values

head() is useful for a first sample, but a person inspecting a 37-row source can use to_string(index=False) to prevent middle rows from being replaced by an ellipsis. Before correcting a category column, inspect its raw values and counts. value_counts(dropna=False, sort=False) includes missingness and retains first-appearance order. Convert the Series to a two-column table when the result needs named fields.

print(df.to_string(index=False, line_width=200))

district_counts = (
    df["district"]
    .value_counts(dropna=False, sort=False)
    .rename_axis("district")
    .reset_index(name="records")
)
print(district_counts.to_string(index=False, formatters={"district": repr}))

One column is a Series; multiple columns form a DataFrame

df[\"registered\"] is a one-dimensional Series. df[[\"registered\"]] is a two-dimensional DataFrame with one column. Column names must match exactly. Arithmetic between Series applies across corresponding rows.

3.1.4 pandas — column calculations and CSV output

assign() creates a new DataFrame with a calculated column without directly changing the source df. Do not interpret a final result before deciding how zero denominators, missing values, and invalid values should behave. Lesson 3.3 examines those quality decisions.

report = df.assign(
    completion_rate=df["completed"] / df["registered"] * 100
)
print(report[["centre_name", "completion_rate"]].head())

Distinguish the index from an operational identifier

The index displayed at the left is a pandas row label, not centre_id. With index=False, exporting to CSV does not add that non-business index as another column. Inspect the saved path and header afterward.

3.1.5 Diagnose loading problems by cause

For FileNotFoundError, inspect the working directory and candidate paths. If everything becomes one column, inspect the delimiter. For mojibake or UnicodeDecodeError, inspect encoding. If a numeric column becomes text, inspect spaces, units, and invalid values. Record the input and loading assumptions before changing values.

3.1.6 Transfer the example to another table

Create a DataFrame from the centre records in 2.3, save it to CSV, and load it again. Compare shape, column names, identifiers, and count totals before and after, then add attendance_rate and completion_rate. Lesson 3.2 selects the rows and columns that answer a question.

activities.content:
Translate an analysis question into displayed columns and row conditions

3.2.1 Separate a question into displayed columns and row conditions

Lesson 3.1 loaded the CSV and established its shape, names, types, and missingness. Now express “which observations, viewed through which fields?” in code. Filtering must not silently select convenient rows. Keep the question, conditions, source count, and matching count connected so another person can reproduce the same subset.

Validate required columns and separate partial conditions

For “show centre names in February and March with at least 30 registrations and attendance below 80%,” identify display columns, month membership, a registration lower bound, and an attendance-rate upper bound. Before processing, compare required names with df.columns and report any missing columns.

required = {"month", "centre_name", "registered", "attended"}
missing = required - set(df.columns)
if missing:
    raise KeyError(sorted(missing))

Select the fields needed for the result

df[\"registered\"] is a one-column Series; df[[\"month\", \"registered\"]] is a DataFrame. Names must match exactly. Distinguish columns needed to calculate a condition from those that must appear in the result.

3.2.2 Select rows and columns with loc and iloc

loc[row condition, column names] uses index labels and named columns, leaving analytical meaning visible. iloc[row positions, column positions] uses zero-based positions and is useful for checks such as first rows. Index labels are not guaranteed to be 0, 1, 2, so do not confuse labels with positions.

3.2.3 Turn comparisons into Boolean masks

df[\"registered\"] >= 30 returns a Boolean Series aligned with the source index. A `True` row matches. mask.sum() counts matches. Recording source and result counts helps detect a reversed comparison or incorrect boundary.

large = df["registered"] >= 30
print(large.head())
print("Matching rows:", int(large.sum()))
result = df.loc[large, ["month", "centre_name", "registered"]]

3.2.4 Build compound conditions with Boolean logic

Use Python and, or, and not for individual Boolean values. For row-wise pandas Series use &, |, and ~, with each comparison in parentheses. Using and with a Series asks for one truth value for the whole Series and raises an error.

large = report["registered"] >= 30
low_rate = report["attendance_rate"] < 80
print("AND:", int((large & low_rate).sum()))
print("OR:", int((large | low_rate).sum()))
print("NOT large:", int((~large).sum()))

Verify AND, OR, and NOT through counts

AND requires both and normally narrows a selection. OR requires either and normally broadens it. NOT reverses truth values. De Morgan’s law says ~(A | B) equals (~A) & (~B). Prefer the form that communicates operational meaning and confirm each partial-mask count.

3.2.5 Express membership, ranges, and missingness

Use isin() for one of several candidates and between() for lower and upper bounds. between() includes both endpoints by default. Match inclusive and exclusive boundaries to words such as “at least,” “at most,” and “below.”

months = report["month"].isin(["2026-02", "2026-03"])
size = report["registered"].between(25, 35, inclusive="both")
subset = report.loc[months & size]

Do not lose missing rows accidentally

A comparison with a missing value is usually False, so a row can disappear without an explanation. Add notna() when a value is required or isna() when investigating missingness, and record the missing count separately. Do not fill or delete values here; retain them as quality issues for Lesson 3.3.

known = report["attended"].notna()
low_known = known & (report["attendance_rate"] < 80)
print(int(low_known.sum()))
print("Missing:", int(report["attended"].isna().sum()))

3.2.6 Filter with masks and verify row counts

Give month, size, rate, and missingness conditions separate names instead of hiding all logic in one expression. Verify their counts, then use loc[final mask, displayed columns]. Use sort_values() when a reproducible result order helps. Report source count, selected count, and condition.

Align masks and rows by index label

pandas aligns a mask with rows by index label, not only physical position. Reusing a mask from another DataFrame or from before an index change can cause misalignment or errors. Normally create the mask from the same DataFrame being selected.

3.2.7 Transfer the conditions to another question

Select February or March centres for Python Foundations with 25–40 registrations, completion below 75%, and a known completion value. Validate columns, display each partial-mask and final count, and sort by month and centre ID. Create a second question with one negated condition and compare counts.

This lesson selects values but does not correct them. Lesson 3.3 handles missingness, inconsistent labels, and impossible values with an audit trail.

activities.name: Lesson 3.3: Data cleaning and audit records
activities.content:
Define the problem before changing the data

3.3.1 Preserve the source and define quality problems

Lesson 3.2 selected the columns and rows needed for a question. Yet correct code can still produce a false conclusion when missing values, inconsistent labels, or impossible relationships are unexplained. Data cleaning is not cosmetic editing or deleting inconvenient rows. Preserve the source, define rules first, detect violations, choose actions, and record the result.

3.3.2 Separate source, working, and analysis-ready data

Keep raw as loaded. Begin processing with clean = raw.copy() and add flags that identify quality problems. Create analysis only from rows meeting the documented readiness rules. These three objects show what changed and what was not used.

raw = pd.read_csv(data_file)
clean = raw.copy()
print("Rows:", len(raw))
print(raw.dtypes)
print(raw.isna().sum())

Inspect types, missingness, categories, and ranges first

Start with dtypes, isna().sum(), category unique() values, and numeric describe(). Those counts are the baseline. Replacing values first prevents you from distinguishing source problems from problems introduced by processing.

3.3.3 Separate type conversion from missingness

pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce") converts invalid numeric text to missing. Compare the missing mask before and after conversion so an original blank and a newly failed conversion remain different issues.

before_missing = clean["attended"].isna()
converted = pd.to_numeric(clean["attended"], errors="coerce")
conversion_failed = converted.isna() & ~before_missing
clean["attended"] = converted
print("Source missing:", int(before_missing.sum()))
print("Conversion failures:", int(conversion_failed.sum()))

Do not confuse missingness with zero

A blank attendance count means “not reported,” not necessarily “nobody attended.” Unsupported filling changes totals, averages, and rates. Flag missingness with isna(), then document whether the row is excluded from a calculation, quarantined for review, or corrected from an authoritative source.

3.3.4 Normalise labels while retaining source values

Whitespace and case differences can split one district into separate groups. Retain the source as district_raw, apply str.strip() and str.title() to the working value, and count affected rows. Do not merge similar-looking words without an agreed rule or mapping.

clean["district_raw"] = clean["district"]
clean["district"] = clean["district"].astype("string").str.strip().str.title()
changed = clean["district_raw"].astype("string") != clean["district"]
print("Changed labels:", int(changed.sum()))

3.3.5 Test ranges, cross-field constraints, and duplicates

Counts and costs have non-negative range rules. This table also defines registered >= attended >= completed. Give each rule a named Boolean mask and display its count. Keep missingness separate from invalidity instead of hiding all problems in one expression.

missing_attended = clean["attended"].isna()
completion_over_attendance = (clean["completed"].notna() & clean["attended"].notna() & (clean["completed"] > clean["attended"]))
negative_cost = clean["material_cost"].notna() & (clean["material_cost"] < 0)
print(int(missing_attended.sum()), int(completion_over_attendance.sum()), int(negative_cost.sum()))

Use a business key to flag every duplicate row

If one record means one centre, month, and course, those three columns form the business key. duplicated(subset=business_key, keep=False) displays every row in a duplicate group. Repeated centres in different months are legitimate, so the definition must precede the test.

business_key = ["centre_id", "month", "course"]
duplicate_key = clean.duplicated(subset=business_key, keep=False)
print("Duplicate-key rows:", int(duplicate_key.sum()))

3.3.6 Build a verification table from quality flags

Detection does not reveal the correct replacement. Correct from an authoritative source, normalise under an explicit rule, or mark a value missing or pending review when evidence is insufficient. Do not guess an impossible completion count. Retain rows and create an analysis_ready flag, then derive the analysis subset separately.

clean["analysis_ready"] = ~(missing_attended | completion_over_attendance | negative_cost | duplicate_key)
analysis = clean.loc[clean["analysis_ready"]].copy()
print("Raw:", len(raw), "ready:", len(analysis), "flagged:", int((~clean["analysis_ready"]).sum()))

3.3.7 Record the audit and validate again

Record the issue, detection rule, affected count, action, and unresolved count. A zero count documents that the check ran. Finally, assert that source rows equal analysis-ready plus flagged rows and that the analysis subset satisfies the same constraints.

assert len(raw) == len(clean)
assert len(clean) == int(clean["analysis_ready"].sum()) + int((~clean["analysis_ready"]).sum())
assert not (analysis["completed"] > analysis["attended"]).any()

Preserve row-level reasons in the verification report

Rule counts do not identify the source rows a reviewer must check. Retain individual flags, append every matching reason in the published order, and select identifying columns into a verification table. Do not discard additional reasons when one row violates several rules.

issue_rules = [(missing_attended, 'missing attended'), (duplicate_key, 'duplicate business key')]
clean['issue'] = ''
for mask, label in issue_rules:
    clean.loc[mask, 'issue'] += label + '; '
records_to_verify = clean.loc[~clean['analysis_ready'], ['month','centre_id','course','issue']]

Validate boundary cases before the project

Keep the source as raw and create the working table with raw.copy(deep=True). Convert numeric columns with pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce"), then evaluate missingness, negatives, and each comparable cross-field constraint separately. Strip business-key whitespace before using duplicated(..., keep=False) to flag every row in a duplicate group.

3.3.8 Transfer quality rules to another dataset

Use the practice CSV to detect missing attendance, district-label variation, and completion above attendance, recording each count. Then check missing completion, attendance above registration, non-positive training hours, negative material cost, and duplicate business keys. Create an audit table containing each rule, count, and proposed action without guessing corrections.

activities.content:
Define what one result row means before aggregation

3.4.1 Define the grain of detail and summary rows

Lesson 3.3 produced analysis-ready detail. Aggregation now compresses those rows into a report. One detail row means centre-month-course; one district summary row means a district; one district-course row means that pair. Define this grain first or even a correct number may be impossible to explain.

3.4.2 Split, count, and combine with groupby

groupby("district") splits matching rows, applies the same named aggregations, and combines results. Named agg() records output meaning; reset_index() restores group keys as ordinary columns.

district = analysis.groupby("district", dropna=False).agg(
 centre_months=("centre_id","size"), centres=("centre_id","nunique"), registered_total=("registered","sum")
).reset_index()

Distinguish what size, count, and nunique count

size counts rows including missing values, count counts non-missing values in a selected column, and nunique counts distinct values. Centre-month records, reported attendance values, and distinct centres are different measures.

3.4.3 Calculate summary statistics and rates

sum measures volume, mean arithmetic centre, median the middle ordered value, min and max endpoints, and std spread around the mean. Extremes can pull the mean, so show count, median, and range. Standard deviation does not explain causes.

analysis.groupby("course")["registered"].agg(["size","sum","mean","median","min","max","std"])

Calculate rates from compatible aggregate totals

Overall course completion is total completed divided by total registered. A simple mean of centre-month rates gives a small and a large record equal weight. It answers about a typical record, not all registered learners. State the denominator in words.

course = analysis.groupby("course").agg(records=("centre_id","size"),registered=("registered","sum"),completed=("completed","sum"),mean_row_rate=("completion_rate","mean"),material_cost=("material_cost","sum"))
course["overall_completion_rate"] = course["completed"] / course["registered"] * 100
course["cost_per_completion"] = course["material_cost"] / course["completed"]

For Python Foundations in the practice data, the simple mean row rate is about 71.9%, while 290 total completions divided by 400 total registrations is 72.5%. Similar values still have different definitions.

Preserve comparison hierarchy with multiple keys

groupby(["district","course"]) creates one row per pair. This differs from district-only grain. Do not add or average incompatible grains without defining their relationship.

3.4.4 Build reproducible rankings from multiple conditions

Sort the primary and secondary measures descending, then a stable ID ascending. The final key resolves ties reproducibly; rank before rounding display values.

ranked = summary.sort_values(['average','days','id'], ascending=[False,False,True])

Save purpose-specific CSVs and validate them after re-reading

Save a verification table and a priority summary separately, then re-read and reconcile column order, row counts, and the first priority. Inspecting only the pre-save variable does not validate the submitted product.

3.4.5 Check the denominator and 100% total of proportions

Course share within a district divides district-course registrations by that district total. The grand total answers another question. transform("sum") aligns denominators, and within-district shares should sum to 100%.

dc["district_total"] = dc.groupby("district")["registered"].transform("sum")
dc["share"] = dc["registered"] / dc["district_total"] * 100

3.4.6 Reconcile aggregation, saving, and re-reading

Grouped record, registered, completed, and material-cost totals must sum back to analysis detail. Assertions expose omitted or double-counted data. Attach counts to averages and do not interpret a small-group difference as proof of cause or superiority.

assert int(course["records"].sum()) == len(analysis)
assert course["registered"].sum() == analysis["registered"].sum()
assert course["completed"].sum() == analysis["completed"].sum()

Put a conditional count into named aggregation

Create a row-level Boolean condition, then sum True values within each group. The decision and its count remain separately inspectable.

operational = analysis.assign(low_completion=analysis['completion_rate'] < 75)
summary = operational.groupby('course').agg(low_records=('low_completion','sum'))

3.4.7 Transfer aggregation and ranking to another decision

By month and course, calculate record count, distinct centres, registered, attended and completed totals, overall completion rate, material cost, and cost per completion. State denominators, compare with mean row rate, reconcile grand totals, and identify a small-count comparison.

You have reached the lesson goal when you can define grain, select count and summary functions, aggregate rate components, group by multiple keys, calculate proportions, and reconcile the result.

activities.content:
Define the question and plotted grain before chart type

A chart is evidence communication, not decoration. Aggregate detail to category grain for comparison or ordered time grain for trends, inspect the plotted table, then draw.

Bars compare category magnitudes

Use bars for a few unordered categories. Compute overall rates from total completed and registered, sort deliberately, and normally start the length axis at zero. A 70% baseline exaggerates 72% versus 74%.

ax.barh(course["course"],course["completion_rate"]); ax.set(xlabel="Completion rate (%)"); ax.set_xlim(0,100)

Lines show ordered time change

Convert month to date, sort chronologically, and expose missing periods. Joining only observed months can imply continuous observation. Lines across unordered categories invent an in-between path.

Scatter plots examine two quantitative variables

Each point links two values from one record. Clusters and unusual points are visible, but association does not establish causation; centre size, month, or course may affect both.

Histograms show one quantitative distribution

Histograms count adjacent numeric bins; bars compare separate categories. Bin width changes the visible pattern, so inspect alternatives and state sample size.

Label title, axes, units, legend, and colour

Name the comparison and units. Use legends only for multiple series, do not rely on colour alone, and use contrast, line style, or direct labels. Avoid 3D and decorative area distortion.

Disclose scale, order, and missingness

Axis range and ordering alter impressions. If a narrow range is useful for a line, disclose it and state the absolute difference. Apply consistent order and never silently convert missing periods to zero.

Reconcile the plotted table

Display the chart table and assert that totals match analysis detail. A chart does not validate its source. Keep aggregation and plotting code, and optionally save a reproducible image with savefig().

assert course["registered"].sum()==analysis["registered"].sum()
assert course["completed"].sum()==analysis["completed"].sum()

Write observation, numbers, scope, and limitation

“Overall completion was 72.5% for Python Foundations and about 73.1% for Digital Skills, a difference of about 0.6 percentage points.” Then state that only 22 analysis-ready centre-months are included and learner mix and course difficulty are uncontrolled, so cause or superiority is not established.

From worked example to transfer

Create monthly registrations as a line, course cost per completion as bars, and registrations versus completion rate as scatter. State question, grain, axes, units, and n. Write four evidence sentences and reject one misleading scale version.

You have reached the goal when chart choice follows the question, plotted data reconciles, scale and missingness are visible, and claims include numbers and limitations.

activities.name: Lesson 12: Processing larger CSV files in chunks
activities.content:
When the file no longer feels small

Estimated study time: 3 hours

Learning objectives

  • Estimate whether a file fits in memory
  • Read only needed columns with explicit types
  • Aggregate a CSV in chunks
  • Reconcile chunk results with independent totals

“Big data” is relative to the available computer. The professional habit is to reduce data early, preserve an audit trail, and validate the final totals. Start with file size, columns, types, row count, missingness, and the question you need to answer.

import pandas as pd

totals = {}
row_count = 0
for chunk in pd.read_csv(
    "transactions.csv",
    usecols=["district", "amount"],
    dtype={"district": "category", "amount": "float64"},
    chunksize=100_000,
):
    row_count += len(chunk)
    part = chunk.groupby("district", observed=True)["amount"].sum()
    for district, amount in part.items():
        totals[district] = totals.get(district, 0) + amount

print("Rows processed:", row_count)
print(totals)

Validation checklist

  1. Compare processed row count with the source expectation.
  2. Count rejected or missing amounts.
  3. Compare the grand total with a second calculation on a small known fixture.
  4. Record file name, date, filters, and cleaning decisions.

Privacy and proportionality

Do not collect personal data merely because storage is available. Remove identifiers not needed for the question, restrict access, and prefer aggregated reporting where possible.

Connection: variables hold running totals; conditions validate rows; loops process chunks; dictionaries merge group results; functions make checks reusable; pandas performs column and group operations; charts communicate the final aggregate.

activities.section_name: 1.3 Basic scalar types, conversion, and arithmetic
activities.content:
Similar appearance does not mean the same kind of value

Lesson 2 established that a name refers to a value. The next question is what kind of value it is. 34 and "34" look similar on screen, but the first is an integer for calculation and the second is a two-character string. A type determines sensible operations and possible results.

print(34, type(34))
print(82.5, type(82.5))
print("34", type("34"))
print(True, type(True))
print(None, type(None))
TypeExampleRepresents
int34A whole integer
float82.5A numeric value with fractional form
str"North"A sequence of characters
boolTrue, FalseA truth value
NoneTypeNoneThe special absence-of-value object

type() inspects the value that exists now. None is not zero or empty text; it is a distinct value representing absence. Booleans are developed with conditions later, but they are already recognisable as a separate type.

Seven arithmetic operators process numeric values

Numeric types support addition +, subtraction -, multiplication *, division /, floor division //, remainder %, and exponentiation **.

ExpressionResultTypical meaning
10 + 313Total
10 - 37Difference
10 * 330Equal groups
10 / 33.333…Rate or average
10 // 33Complete groups
10 % 31Remainder
10 ** 2100Exponentiation

In Python 3, / normally returns a float even for integer operands. // is floor division rather than a general “remove the decimal part” operation. This course first uses positive quantities, where it can represent complete boxes or groups.

Precedence and parentheses communicate calculation meaning

Exponentiation, multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction are evaluated in order. 2 + 3 * 4 is 14; (2 + 3) * 4 is 20. Parentheses also prevent a reader from misunderstanding the work meaning.

books = 53
per_box = 12
full_boxes = books // per_box
remaining_books = books % per_box
print("Full boxes:", full_boxes)
print("Books remaining:", remaining_books)

Fifty-three books make four complete boxes with five books left. Five boxes are required to hold every book, so the result of // must not automatically be labelled “boxes required”. Relate every numeric result to the quantity requested by the task.

Convert explicitly instead of assuming a type

Numbers received from a CSV or input form may be strings. Numeric 4 cannot be added directly to text "36". Use int() for an integer, float() for a fractional numeric value, and str() for display text.

learners_text = "36"
learners = int(learners_text)
print(learners + 4)

cost_text = "487.50"
cost = float(cost_text)
print(cost, type(cost))

Text that cannot represent the requested type raises ValueError. int("12.5") fails; use float("12.5") first, then decide whether losing the fractional part is genuinely appropriate.

bool() also needs care. bool("False") does not interpret the word; it returns True because the string is non-empty. External "True" and "False" text requires explicit content-aware conversion.

Successful execution is not enough: validate the number

Division by zero raises ZeroDivisionError. A completion rate for zero registrations or cost per completion for zero completions requires a policy, later implemented with a condition, rather than unprotected division.

Many decimal float values are binary approximations, so 0.1 + 0.2 may display as 0.30000000000000004. round() can prepare a reporting display, but rounding does not repair invalid data. State the chosen precision and why it is suitable.

From guided example to transfer

For 29 completions from 36 registrations, the completion rate is completed / registered * 100. Keep numerator and denominator in the intended order and round the report to one decimal place.

registered = 36
completed = 29
completion_rate = completed / registered * 100
print("Completion rate:", round(completion_rate, 1), "%")

For transfer practice, pack 53 books at 12 per box and display complete boxes, remainder, and boxes required for every book. Then convert material-cost text "487.50", divide it by 30 registrations, and display cost per learner to two decimals. Explain what happens when registrations are zero.

After this lesson, you can distinguish value and type and explain seven arithmetic operators, precedence, explicit conversion, and common numeric errors. Strings, input, and formatted output come next as a separate lesson before decisions with conditions.

Estimated study time: about 2.5 hours
